claim: Petitions to the county property value appeals board are filed with the board clerk after tax statements are mailed and by December 31.
The board may convene on or after the first Monday in February and must adjourn no later than April 15.
The board hears petitions to reduce real market value, assessed value, or maximum assessed value as of January 1.
If a taxpayer may appeal to the property value appeals board, no Tax Court appeal is allowed until the board order issues; Tax Court appeal is from the board order.
An appeal to the Tax Court from a county property value appeals board order must be filed within 30 days of the order mailing, publication or delivery date.
Real and personal property is valued at 100 percent of real market value; assessed value is generally the lesser of maximum assessed value or real market value.
Maximum assessed value equals 103 percent of prior-year assessed value or 100 percent of prior-year maximum assessed value, whichever is greater.
A person aggrieved by an omitted-property assessment may appeal to the Tax Court within 90 days after the roll correction.

Oregon's statutory homestead exemption protects a homestead from execution, judgment liens and debts up to $150,000 (combined $300,000 for two or more household judgment debtors), indexed annually.
For child support, spousal support or restitution judgments the homestead exemption is $40,000 ($50,000 combined).
The homestead must be the actual abode of and occupied by the owner or the owner's spouse, parent or child.
The exemption is effective without a claim by the judgment debtor and extends to sale proceeds held up to one year with intent to buy another homestead.
The exemption applies to a manufactured dwelling, floating home, and a purchaser's interest under a land sale contract.
Separate from the creditor exemption, Oregon offers property tax deferral on an owner-occupied homestead for qualifying seniors/persons with a disability (ORS 311.666 to 311.701).

A city, county, district or other political subdivision may not impose a tax or fee on the transfer of a fee estate in real property or measured by consideration paid.
The prohibition does not apply to a tax in effect and operative on March 31, 1997.
The prohibition does not apply to a fee under ORS 203.148.
Fees or charges that become due at the time of transfer are not a transfer tax unless imposed on the right, privilege or act of transferring title.
The prohibition does not apply to a tax or fee if the ORS 205.323 recording fee for the instrument is less than $107.

The default may be cured up to five days before the last-set sale date by paying the amount due plus costs and fees ($1,000 combined trustee and attorney fees for residential trust deeds, or actual if less).
A trustee's sale forecloses and terminates interests of noticed persons, who may not redeem from the purchaser.
No deficiency action may follow a trustee's sale or judicial foreclosure of a residential trust deed.
Judicial foreclosure of a lien is by suit; a complaint on a residential trust deed must attach resolution-conference compliance documents.
A judgment of foreclosure orders the property sold; judicial-sale redemption follows execution-sale rules (ORS 18.860 to 18.993).

The affidavit must describe estate property, including a legal description of any real property, and list heirs, devisees and creditors.

After the first year, a landlord may end a month-to-month tenancy for a qualifying reason, including accepting a purchase offer from a buyer who will occupy as primary residence.

A landlord ending a tenancy under subsection (5) must state the reason and pay one month's rent, except landlords owning four or fewer units.
Terminating in violation makes the landlord liable for three months' rent plus actual damages.
If the dwelling shares a property with the landlord's residence (two units or fewer), 30 days' notice applies when a buyer will occupy.

Oregon adopted the Uniform Real Property Transfer on Death Act (ORS 93.948 to 93.979).
An individual may transfer property to designated beneficiaries effective at death via a transfer on death deed, with primary and alternate beneficiaries.
The deed must state transfer occurs at death, name the beneficiary, and be recorded before the transferor's death in the county deed records.
A transfer on death deed is revocable regardless of contrary provisions.
Revocation must be by recorded instrument or inconsistent deed, not by act on the deed.
Capacity is the same as for a will; contests must be commenced within 18 months after death.
The estate may enforce creditor claims against transferred property if the probate estate is insufficient, within 18 months.
